Load-to-body-weight and yoke hours are genuine welfare levers — I don't want to undersell them — but they capture a fraction of the burden, and lameness in particular is frequently caused by the very work you're logging. The protocol as drafted can't see it.

Four additions that fit on a farmer-completed log:

- **Lameness at yoking.** A three-point walk check (sound / shortened stride or head nod / unwilling to bear weight) recorded before work. Farmers already notice this and act on it economically, because a lame ox works badly.
- **Visible harness wounds.** Yes/no at yoking, with location.
- **Water offered during the working period.** Yes/no per working day.
- **Any animal withdrawn from work for injury or illness,** with dates. The farmer already has this information, and it's the closest free proxy for the health dimension you'll get.

You'll hear "we can't validate farmer-scored lameness." Partly true — and it matters less than it sounds, because these entries give your auditor something falsifiable. A log showing zero lameness for twelve months across a working buffalo pair is a flag, checkable against the animals standing in the yard. That's a stronger verification posture than you currently have, where "log completeness" rewards diligent transcription and a farmer who invents plausible numbers scores better than one who records honestly and imperfectly.

**Two weaknesses inside your own frame**

*Whose body weight, measured how?* A farmer eyeballing a bullock's weight is routinely off by 15–20%, which swallows the threshold whole. Specify the estimation method — girth-length formula, or a published breed-and-age table — or the indicator is unfalsifiable in both directions.

*Daily hours yoked has no threshold at all.* You record the variable a farmer can report most accurately, the one most closely tied to exhaustion, and then never score it. Even a crude cap on continuous hours without a rest-and-water break adds real signal for zero cost. Relatedly, "fewer than 10 working days per quarter" teaches the arithmetic: a farmer who knows the tolerance logs nine and stops. Requiring a written reason at the 2-point tier at least generates something an auditor can probe.

**The claim is the exposed element**

Since you asked how it lands: "verified working-animal welfare" doesn't describe what you measure. Load and hours are two inputs to welfare; the protocol is silent on the most prevalent harm in the population. Two risks, neither of them an advocacy framing:

Unsubstantiated welfare claims are what consumer-protection and green-claims regimes have been tightening around, and a claim whose scope is far narrower than its wording is the standard fact pattern.

More to the point, it sets up the failure mode you're trying to avoid. The likeliest route to sinking this standard isn't an advocacy group saying your logbook is incomplete — everyone knows logbooks are incomplete. It's a journalist photographing a severely lame ox on a farm carrying a "verified welfare" label. The narrow claim survives that story. The broad one doesn't, and it takes credibility from every other scheme with it.

The fix is free: "verified load and working-hours limits," or "verified draft-load standard." If marketing needs the word welfare, "working-animal welfare: load and hours verified" carries its own qualifier. Worth the fight, since you're the one who'll be quoted defending the wording.

**Why now rather than at revision**

The indicator set becomes the working definition of draft-animal welfare for this sector. Adjacent standards will copy it; the next revision will start from it. Omissions harden into blind spots, and post-adoption revision is harder than pre-adoption drafting. You're three weeks out and you hold the pen.

Two things make reopening the draft survivable. First, build the tiering in explicitly: what you have becomes Level 1 (farmer-logged, smallholder-priced), with Level 2 specified for on-site assessment even if nobody qualifies in year one. That puts the incremental path on the record, so you're presenting a floor as a floor rather than as a ceiling, and gives larger producers who can absorb assessor fees somewhere to go. Second, consider a sampled-verification layer — a small percentage of certified households get an assessor visit that spot-checks self-reported lameness and water access against observation. That costs real budget, and it's the one item here that isn't free, so it may be the piece you defer; but it's what would let you say the farmer-report indicators are calibrated rather than trusted, and it scales with the scheme rather than with the animal count.

**The thing to say out loud to the committee**

The pilot collected the same logs from thirty-odd households and tested nothing about welfare outcomes. Better said by you in the drafting memo than discovered by someone else later. And it frames well: the pilot demonstrated that farmer-completed logs are feasible at scale, which is exactly the finding that supports adding cheap observable content to those logs. The pilot's actual result argues for the expansion, not against it.

If it's useful, I can draft the four added indicator lines with scoring tiers and the auditor cross-check language, in the same register as your existing wording.
